spatial_claims.claim: D is a point within circle ABC
DA, DB, DC are straight lines from D to the circumference with DA = DB = DC
E is the centre of circle ABC, distinct from D
Line DE is produced in both directions to meet the circumference at F and G
FG passes through centre E, so FG is a diameter of circle ABC
D lies on diameter FG and is not the centre of the circle
From D on diameter FG (not the centre), only two equal straight lines can fall from D on the circle (by 3.7)

configuration_map: D: inside circle ABC (Step 1); lies on line DE which is extended to diameter FG, so D is on diameter FG strictly between F and G (Step 3); D is not the centre E (Step 2). E: centre of circle ABC (Step 2); lies on diameter FG (Step 3); distinct from D. F, G: on circumference of circle ABC; endpoints of diameter FG (Step 3). A, B, C: on circumference of circle ABC; equidistant from D (Step 1). The key spatial fact is that D lies on diameter FG but is not the centre, which is exactly the configuration required for Proposition 3.7 to apply.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. D is inside the circle and on diameter FG (since line DE through the centre is extended to the circumference). The application of 3.7 to point D on diameter FG (not the centre) is geometrically valid. The reductio correctly derives a contradiction between 3.7's conclusion (at most two equal lines from D to the circle) and the hypothesis (three equal lines). No angle decompositions, no interior/exterior conflicts, no conflicting point positions.
